narrative:
The model predicted a 56.3% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your class rank at the end of your third year was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. Placing in the first decile (bottom 10%) of your class is well below the average of roughly the sixth decile among students who were accepted, signaling that your academic performance in law school was significantly weaker than most successful applicants.

Your LSAT score of 35.5 worked in the opposite direction, modestly pulling the prediction toward passing. While this score is a bit below the 37.2 average of accepted students, it still provided some positive signal. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.40 also nudged the outcome slightly toward success. At 3.40 you actually outperformed the 3.23 average of accepted applicants, which helped offset some of the risk.

Taken together, the model concluded that your relatively low third-year class ranking outweighed the encouraging signals from your LSAT and college grades, resulting in a failure probability high enough to deny admission.

What you should do next is focus on strengthening your academic record. Improving your class rank in the remaining years, or retaking the LSAT if you can raise it meaningfully, would directly address the factor that hurt your application most. Many students successfully reapply after showing clearer evidence of strong law-school performance.
